p: Passwords are hard to remember, easy to reuse and easy to steal through phishing. Passkeys are a newer sign-in method designed to fix those problems. Major platforms and browsers now support them, and more users are encountering the prompt to create one. If you run a website or app with logins, it is worth understanding whether and how to offer them.

A passkey is based on a pair of cryptographic keys. When a user registers, their device creates a private key that never leaves the device and a public key that is stored on your server. To sign in, the device proves it holds the private key, usually after the user unlocks it with a fingerprint, face scan or device PIN. There is no shared secret to type, so there is nothing for a phishing site or a leaked database to capture.

list: Phishing resistance: a passkey only works on the genuine site it was created for.
Nothing valuable to steal from your server: only public keys are stored.
Faster sign-in: users tap or scan instead of typing and resetting passwords.
Fewer support requests: there are no forgotten-password emails to handle.
Device changes and recovery: users need a safe way back in if they lose a device. Many passkeys sync through the platform's account, but you still need a fallback.
Mixed audiences: older devices and some browsers lag, so you will support passwords alongside passkeys for a while.
User understanding: the idea is new, so clear wording and prompts matter.
Shared devices and business accounts: decide how to handle them.
Keep existing login working and add passkeys as an option after sign-in, for example by offering to create one.
Use a well-maintained library or an identity provider that supports the WebAuthn standard instead of building the cryptography yourself.
Pair it with recovery options such as email verification or backup codes.
Measure adoption and sign-in success, then promote passkeys more prominently as confidence grows.
Keep multi-factor authentication for sensitive actions such as changing payout details.

p: For apps with many returning customers, financial or personal data, or heavy password-reset support, passkeys are a strong improvement. For a small internal tool, a good identity provider with MFA may be enough. Either way, the direction is clear: reducing reliance on passwords makes accounts safer.

list: Passkeys replace typed passwords with device-based cryptographic sign-in.
They resist phishing and reduce support load.
Roll them out as an addition first, with solid recovery options.

h: A worked example: adding passkeys to an existing app
p: A subscription app has thousands of users who sign in with email and password. Support receives a steady flow of reset requests, and the team worries about reused passwords leaked from other sites.

Rather than replace passwords, the team adds passkeys gradually. After a user signs in the normal way, a prompt offers to create a passkey on that device, with a short explanation that next time they can sign in with a fingerprint or face scan. The team uses a maintained library supporting the WebAuthn standard and stores only the public key and a credential identifier on its server.

They keep email-based recovery and offer backup codes, so a user who loses a phone can still get back in. Sensitive actions such as changing payout details still ask for an extra check. Over time, as more users adopt passkeys, the team promotes them more prominently on the login screen and tracks the drop in password resets.

list: Removing passwords too early: locking out users on older devices or browsers.
Weak recovery: making account recovery the easiest way for an attacker to take over an account.
Rolling your own cryptography: building the protocol from scratch instead of using vetted libraries.
Confusing wording: using technical terms that make users hesitate.
Skipping testing: not trying sign-in across different devices, browsers and operating systems.
Forgetting admin and staff accounts: leaving the most powerful accounts on the weakest login method.
Confirm your login library or identity provider supports passkeys.
Keep existing sign-in methods working at first.
Offer passkey creation after a successful normal sign-in.
Design recovery with verified email, backup codes or support checks.
Test on the main browsers, phones and operating systems your users have.
Write short, plain-language prompts that explain the benefit.
Track adoption, failures and support requests, then adjust.

p: What happens if a user loses their phone? Many passkeys sync through the user's platform account, and you should also provide recovery options so users are not locked out.
Are passkeys the same as biometrics? Not exactly. A fingerprint or face scan unlocks the passkey on the device, but the biometric data stays on the device and is not sent to your server.

Are passkeys safer than passwords with multi-factor authentication? They are strongly resistant to phishing because they only work on the genuine site. Many security experts see them as a step forward, though a well-run multi-factor setup is also a solid choice.
Do my customers need new hardware? Usually not. Many current phones and computers support passkeys, though very old devices or browsers may not.
